blocks.text: The newspaper lay open on Laura's table.
Yesterday she had folded the photograph inward. Now she could see herself every time she crossed the room: the mask, her lifted arm, the fire climbing behind her.
She remembered the seller reaching for the burning papers. His sleeve had been rough beneath her fingers when she pulled him away.
Then she read the headline again.
LAVA LIPS TORCHES NEWSSTAND.
The headline had followed her home. So had Flaming Head's admission that his landing had changed her. Laura pushed her chair in hard and went to the dresser.
The costume lay folded on the dresser. She picked it up.
This time, before leaving, she put her glasses in their case, tied back her hair and fastened the mask. She left the newspaper open.
The Army demonstration was that afternoon. Daniel stood three people back from the rope and watched a soldier turn a blue toggle.

Beyond the rope, a metal equipment chest sat inside a painted white square. The soldier stood several feet away, holding a gray machine by two handles. Copper rings surrounded its short barrel. An analog meter quivered beneath a small glass window.
“Clear of the marked area,” the officer beside him said.
The soldier checked both sides of the square. Then he pressed a button beneath his right thumb.
A pale flash washed over the chest.
Where it had stood, something no larger than a matchbox rested on the pavement.
The crowd leaned forward.
Daniel did too, but his eyes stayed on the soldier's hands.
blocks.alt: Daniel leans over the spectator rope, watching a soldier operate the copper-ringed shrink ray as a tiny equipment chest glows inside the white demonstration square.

blocks.text: The officer waited until everyone had seen. The soldier moved the toggle from blue to red, aimed at the little chest and pressed the same button.
The chest filled the square again.
Daniel's fingers closed on the rope.
At the far side of the yard, an olive-drab tank stood beside a wide service gate. Its hatch was open. A soldier climbed down from the turret and joined two others by a transport truck.
Daniel looked from the ray to the tank.
“You're doing it again,” Luke whispered from behind the canvas side of a display truck.
Daniel stepped back from the spectators until the truck hid him too.
“Doing what?”
“That face.”
“I've seen the controls.”
Luke watched the soldier put the ray down. “Try remembering what we need it for.”
Daniel was already measuring the distance from the table to the gate.
Luke watched him for another moment before rising behind the canvas.
Laura noticed the woman outside the bakery first.
She had been coming toward her with a paper bag held against her coat. Her eyes went to Laura's mask, then down to the flames along her sides.
The woman stopped so abruptly that the man behind her nearly walked into her.
“That's her,” she said.
Laura heard the whisper that followed.
“Lava Lips.”
Her shoulders tightened. She waited for laughter.
Instead, the woman moved against the bakery window. The man stepped around a parking meter to give Laura room.
Laura passed between them.
At the next doorway, someone stopped talking. Two boys who had been taking up most of the sidewalk moved into single file.
She had meant to close her coat before reaching the shops. She left it open.
Inside a small grocery, a customer at the counter looked over his shoulder. His eyes stayed on her mouth.
“I can wait,” he told the clerk.
Laura stopped behind him. “I only need these.”
She held up a loaf of bread and a small carton of milk.
The man moved aside.
The clerk rang up her purchase quickly. A coin slipped from his fingers and struck the counter. He caught it on the second try.
Laura could have told him she was not going to do anything.
She watched him gather her change instead.
He placed it beside her hand without touching her glove.
“Thank you,” she said.
He nodded twice.
blocks.alt: Costumed Laura walks slowly through a shopping street as frightened pedestrians make room, a pleased smile beginning on her face.

blocks.text: Outside, she walked more slowly. Nobody bumped her shoulder. Nobody made her squeeze past.
She took the long way home.
The demonstration ended with questions.
Daniel stayed until the crowd began leaving through the pedestrian gate. He drifted toward the display truck as the soldier carried the ray to a padded case on a folding table.

The table stood on the far side of the truck, screened from the officer by its canvas body. Stacked crates left a narrow approach at the rear. Daniel had watched the soldier set the ray down twice, leaving its handles upright.
“Far end,” he murmured.
Luke looked toward the service gate. Beyond it lay a narrow lane between the yard and a warehouse wall.
“And don't wait for me to ask twice,” Daniel added.
“I wasn't planning to.”
Luke slipped behind the truck.
A moment later, a shout came from the far corner of the display.
A blond head rose above a stack of wooden crates. Sunlight caught the bolts along its steel jaw.
“Afternoon,” Luke said.
The officer turned. The soldier beside the case went around the front of the truck to see what had appeared above the crates.
Daniel moved.
He lifted the ray by its handles. It was heavier than he expected; one corner struck the padded lid.
The soldier heard it and turned. He could see Daniel through the gap beside the crates, but the truck blocked the direct route back.
“Put that down!”
Daniel backed toward the tank. The barrel swung past the truck before he steadied it. He could see blue beneath the toggle.
The empty hatch gaped above the turret. No one stood beside the tracks.
He pressed the button.
The flash made him blink.
A tiny tank sat on the pavement.
Daniel stared for half a second. A boot scraped against the crates as the soldier tried the narrow gap, then went around instead.
He crouched, trapped the ray against his knees and picked up the tank. Its little gun caught against the opening of his coat pocket. He turned it sideways and pushed it in.
Luke swept around the end of the truck.
“You've got it. Move!”
blocks.alt: Daniel holds the miniature empty tank and stolen ray as bodyless Luke rejoins him near the Army display service exit.

blocks.text: Daniel lurched through the service gate with both hands on the ray. Behind him, the officer called for the gate to be closed.
A soldier ran along the outside fence to cut him off at the street.
“This way!” Luke snapped.
He vanished into the gap behind the warehouse.
Daniel followed. The passage was too narrow to run with the ray across him. He turned sideways, scraped a handle against brick and heard footsteps pass the opening behind them.
At the other end, Luke peered around a rubbish bin.
“Wait.”
Daniel's breath rasped in his throat.
A truck engine started in the lane beyond. Luke watched it pull out, then dipped beneath the edge of its canvas cover.
“Now.”
They crossed behind the moving truck and went down the steps to a recessed loading door. Daniel crouched below street level until the shouting grew fainter.
He kept one hand over the tank in his pocket.
Luke hovered beside the steps.
“Well?”
Daniel looked up.
“It worked,” he whispered.
Luke turned away.
Two days later, Laura stopped at the burned newsstand.
Someone had cleared the sidewalk. The wooden roof still leaned crookedly above the counter. Black streaks ran down the boards where the water had dried.
The seller was pulling bent metal strips from a box. He looked up when her shadow crossed the counter.
His hands stopped.
Laura remembered the heat against her face. The newspapers curling. His sleeve in her fist.
She had thought of those things over and over after the fire. This time she waited for the sick feeling to follow.
It did not.
“You're back,” he said.
“I was passing.”
He set the strip down. His gaze dropped to her mouth.
She could see the place where his sign had fallen. Only two hooks remained.
“I've got to replace all of it,” he said.
Laura looked at the blackened counter.
“Nobody was hurt,” she said.
“No.” He looked down into the box. “Nobody was.”
For a moment, she thought he might ask her for money. Her jaw tightened before he said anything else.
But he only shifted the box farther from the edge.
The seller looked at her mouth again.
blocks.alt: Laura meets the frightened newsstand seller’s gaze across his charred counter without offering an apology.

blocks.text: Laura let him.
“Well,” she said. “I won't keep you.”
She walked away before he could answer.
At the corner, two people recognized her and moved apart. She passed through the space they left.
By the time she reached the next street, she was no longer thinking about the missing sign.
Daniel returned to the old building after dark.
He had wrapped the ray in a blanket. Even so, its corners knocked against his legs on the stairs.
Luke went ahead through the broken pane beside the upstairs landing. From inside, he lifted the loose window catch with the edge of his jaw.
Daniel shoved the sash up and climbed through.
The upstairs laboratory smelled of dust and damp wood. Cabinets still held wire, jars of fasteners and instruments with cracked cases. A freestanding bench carried an old vise.
The police had taken the collector, cage, restraints and records from the separate basement workshop. What remained up here was less impressive, but Daniel could use it.
He unplugged a bench meter and wound its cord around it.
Luke watched him inspect the blue toggle.
“Not the room,” he said.
Daniel looked up. “What?”
“Don't point that thing at the whole room while I'm in it.”
“I'm taking the equipment.”
He checked behind the bench, making sure nothing connected it to the wall. Then he stepped back and aimed.
After the flash, the bench lay on the floor like a piece of doll furniture.
Daniel picked it up with both hands. He laughed once, quietly.

They worked until the upstairs room held bare patches of floor and dusty outlines. Daniel packed the little cabinets and benches in an old instrument case, separating them with folded cloth. Anything attached to the building stayed behind.
When he closed the case, Luke looked around the empty room.
“All of it in one case?”
Daniel patted the lid. “It fits now.”
Outside, they took back streets toward a row of industrial buildings Daniel had inspected while waiting for the demonstration.

One workshop had a faded FOR LEASE board in an upstairs window. A side door hung crookedly where someone had already forced it. Daniel pushed through, then stopped while Luke checked the dark interior.
“No one,” Luke called.
Daniel found a piece of timber and wedged the door shut behind them.
The loading entrance opened onto a broad concrete floor. He cleared broken pallets from it before setting the tiny tank down.
“Back,” he said.
Luke moved behind a brick pillar.
Daniel changed the toggle to red.
The tank returned with a heavy settling creak. One track crushed a splinter he had missed.
For a long moment, Daniel stood beneath its gun and grinned.
Then he began unpacking the case.
Flaming Head was above the rocks when Laura reached the slipway the following afternoon.
She stopped at the top of the concrete slope. He did not come closer.
“I hoped you'd come back,” he said.
She could hear him as clearly as before. His mouth did not move.
“I wasn't coming to practice.”
“All right.”
She went down the slope anyway. The old marks were still in the earth bank. She glanced at them, then at him.
“People know me now.”
“From the newspaper?”
“They get out of my way.”
He watched her face.
“They're frightened,” he said.
“I know.”
“Laura—”
“They're careful around me now,” Laura said. “I like it.”
Flaming Head's flames settled. She held his gaze.
He hovered lower, nearer the edge of the concrete.
“Have you spoken to the man from the newsstand?”
“I saw him.”
“How is he?”
“Alive.”
Flaming Head waited.
“Nobody was hurt,” she said. “It was an accident.”
“He still lost something.”
“So did I.”
The words came easily. She did not have to look away after saying them.
Flaming Head stayed quiet. Once, his silence would have made her plead with him to answer. Now she watched the little face in the fire and wondered why she had ever expected him to understand.
“Maybe I don't want you here.”
She took a step toward him.
He moved back over the rocks, keeping the same distance between them.
Laura stopped.
blocks.alt: Costumed Laura steps toward Flaming Head at the lakeside slipway and watches him withdraw over the rocks.

blocks.text: He had moved because she moved.
She felt the small pleasure of it before she could name it.
“Is that what you want?” he asked. “For me to leave?”
She could have told him to stay. She could have asked another question and watched him struggle to answer it.
Instead, she turned toward the path.
“I don't need another lesson.”
At the top of the slope, she ran a gloved thumb over one of the flame shapes. He had made the whole suit with his light, as easily as though making her something to wear could settle anything.
She let the coat hang open.
This time she did not look back to see whether he followed.
By evening, the workshop held two benches, three cabinets and enough loose equipment to cover most of them.
Much of it was still unplugged. Daniel had found one working wall socket and used it for a lamp.
The tank stood by the loading entrance. Every time he passed it, he touched the metal as if checking it had stayed full size.
Luke hovered above an empty stool.
“You've got your laboratory,” Luke said.
Daniel opened a cabinet. Two drawers stuck. “And tools.”
“So when do we start?”
He tugged harder at the drawer. “Once I've put this in order.”
Luke turned toward the dark windows. Daniel went on searching the cabinet.
Then Daniel reached into his coat and took out the newspaper. The folds had softened from being opened so often.
He spread it beneath the lamp.
Laura's masked face looked up from the photograph. Behind her, the newsstand burned.
blocks.alt: Daniel studies the Lava Lips article beneath a workshop lamp beside restored equipment and a full-size tank while bodyless Luke watches apart.

blocks.text: Luke saw where Daniel's eyes had gone.
“What about her?”
“People will recognize that costume.” Daniel smoothed the page. “Somebody will have seen her.”
“You don't even know her.”
“Not yet.”
Luke drifted away from the stool.
Daniel did not look up.
“Now let's find her.”
